targetWords.definition: To achieve something is to successfully do it after trying hard.
targetWords.example: I was happy that I could achieve my goal.

targetWords.definition: To advise someone is to tell them what to do.
targetWords.example: My mother often advises people about their money.

targetWords.definition: If something happens already, it happens before a certain time. — It is already time for the movie to start. Let's go in.
If something is basic, it is very simple or easy.
targetWords.example: I learned some basic English skills in school today. O' bit [bit] n.

targetWords.definition: ->I ate a bit of chocolate before I went to bed.
targetWords.example: I ate a bit of chocolate before I went to bed.

targetWords.definition: To consider something means to think about it.
targetWords.example: Pete didn't like his job. He considered getting a new one.

targetWords.definition: To destroy means to damage something so badly that it cannot be used.
To entertain someone is to do something that they enjoy.
targetWords.example: The clown entertained the kids at the party.

targetWords.definition: If something is extra, it is more than what is needed.
targetWords.example: The squirrel had extra nuts for the winter.

targetWords.definition: A goal is something you work toward.
targetWords.example: ■Her goal was to become a doctor. /\n # k [20J

targetWords.definition: To lie is to say or write something untrue to deceive someone.
targetWords.example: Whenever Pinocchio lied to his father, his nose grew.

targetWords.definition: Meat is food made of animals.
targetWords.example: ■This piece of meat I'm eating tastes very good.

targetWords.definition: An opinion is a thought about a person or a thing.
targetWords.example: Meg told me her opinion of my story. She said it was not funny.

targetWords.definition: If something is real, it actually exists.
targetWords.example: •The handbag has a stamp on it, so it's real.

targetWords.definition: To reflect is when a surface sends back light, heat, sound or an image.
targetWords.example: Her face was reflected on the smooth glass.

targetWords.definition: To regard someone or something is to think of them in a certain way.
targetWords.example: The boy regarded the girl as a good friend.

targetWords.definition: To serve someone is to give them food or drinks.
targetWords.example: He served us our drinks quickly.

targetWords.definition: A vegetable is a plant used as food.
A war is a big fight between two groups of people.
targetWords.example: Many young men died in the war.

targetWords.definition: If something is worth an amount of money, it costs that amount.
targetWords.example: Our house is worth a lot of money. 123

story.title: The Seven Cities of Gold
story.passage:
Many years ago, a Spanish officer named Coronado heard the story of seven

great cities. "The walls of these cities are made of gold," his friends told him. "The

people eat meat from golden plates and dress in nice clothes," they said. They

called these cities the Seven Cities of Gold. Were the cities real? Coronado never

considered asking his friends.

Coronado thought to himself, "The things in these cities must be worth a lot of

money." So he went to find the Seven Cities of Gold. He took along three hundred

men, many horses, and extra food. They headed west. Coronado wanted to

achieve his goal very badly.

Coronado and his men rode for many days. Then they saw some cities. "We

found the Seven Cities of Gold!" his men yelled, but Coronado wasn't happy. He

had a different opinion. "These can't be the Seven Cities of Gold," he said. " Look,

they're made of dirt!"

Coronado was right. The cities weren't bright and golden. They were dirty and

brown. The people didn't eat meat from golden plates. They ate vegetables from

regular bowls. They wore the most basic clothes.

Coronado regarded the cities as ugly places.

"What happened to the cities of gold?" he thought.

" Did someone destroy them? Was there a war? Did

someone already come and take the gold?"

Coronado and his men and served them food.
